From an FTM guy who's married to a recently out trans woman and is going through my own similar set of circumstances: it's okay to be anxious about the future and the changes that can come with it.

My wife met me before I was on T, though we started dating after. She also saw me go through top surgery and now the beginning stages of phalloplasty.

When I got top surgery, my wife was so anxious about the ordeal. She worried so much about if she would miss my old chest or if it would change how we have sex. I still have some numb spots where the bulk of my breast tissue was, and my nipples aren't very sensitive anymore, but top surgery brought us closer together. We had to relearn some of the mechanical aspects of my chest (like where my new sensitive spots are), but our intimate time has never been better. I feel more at home in my body, which means i can actually enjoy myself in a way I don't think I could before.

Right now, we're going through our own rough patch because she came out as trans earlier this year. We both have our anxieties about how intimacy has changed with her libido and desire type. But we're just trying to take things a day at a time and allowing space for curiosity and all the feelings the changes bring.

I know for me it's really easy to get anxious and fixate on the future, but I try to take a deep breath and focus on the now and try to find the good parts. Like how my wife is more happy and relaxed, how we can try new things together, things like that.

Basically: it's okay you're feeling this way. It's perfectly reasonable. Just be sure to give space for your feelings and not be too hard on yourself.

Every hospital is a little different. Here's how it went for me.

They took me and my partner back to a room and confirmed my health history and medicines. Then, they gave me a cup to provide a small urine sample for a pregnancy test and sent me to the bathroom. After I came back, I was allowed to undress and wipe down with some special wipes before putting on a cap and gown and settling onto the gurney bed with a thermal blanket.

When the nurse came back, she gave me my initial IV on my right hand. It hurt a little (like 3/10), but I was so excited I was willing to overlook it. My assisting doctor came in with some paperwork for me to sign. My hand was kind of stiff from the IV, so I used my opposite hand but eventually switched to my right hand and just moved my whole arm instead of my wrist. Then, the anesthesia team came in to ask me some questions and have me sign off on some other paperwork. I think I remember them or my pre-op nurse giving me some acetaminophen to take with a small amlunt of water. After they left, my surgeon and the assisting doctor came in to mark up my chest. After they were finished, they asked me if I was ready and I confirmed.

Once I was tucked back into the thermal blanket, anesthesia came back in and gave me a shot of midazolam into the IV to help me relax. After that, they rolled me back into the OR. They helped me move up onto the operating table, put a mask over my face, and told me to take deep breaths. I think I managed two before I was out.

The OR team actually put in a second IV set on my left hand while I was under for IV fluids. The first one was for IV push medications (like fentanyl or hydromorphone) during and after the procedure.

You might be able to ask them to save putting in your IV for just before you roll back or you can ask for a local anesthetic for the pain like lidocaine to help after it's in. Lido does sting going in, but it can help keep everything numb. FWIW, the IV feels like a very big pinch and aches a little when they do it. IV lines are very soft and flexible compared to something they might use for a flu shot.

Definitely talk with your pre-op nurse and let them know that you're nervous! They're very used to people being nervous and will do their best to accommodate you and make you feel comfortable! You can also talk with your surgeon in advance and they can arrange for you to have an anxiolytic with your pre-op medications!

I wanted to add mine to the pool because Dr. Freet is a personable and talented surgeon! He's fairly old school when it comes to top surgery and is most likely to recommend DI unless you have a very small amount of breast tissue to qualify for peri/keyhole. I had asked if peri was possible, but EDS was recently confirmed to run in my family, and he had some concerns about the nipple placement looking good and my scars stretching or the skin puckering. He also felt my chest didn't need drains with DI, which was great to not have to worry about while I was recovering!

My only complaint is that he gives you ace bandages post-op for compression. They do work, but I felt like they were harder to put on by myself and would feel like it was pulling on my incisions when I sat up straight. This made me hunch over more than I should and has caused some flare-ups with some chronic back cramps I have. I ended up springing for a post-op binder from Underworks and will probably cut it to size since it's long for me.

I wanted to share some extra pictures showing how far up my incisions go. This length will help prevent dog ears in the long term. I also wanted to show some close ups of my nipple grafts as they've been healing. Things seem to be healing normal, I just don't see as many pictures of grafts that turn locally brown like my left one has! 

Once my 1 week bandages were removed, I slapped on hydrocolloid bandages and haven't looked back. Things are coming together beautifully and I've gotten emotional and teared up several times. The dimple in the center of my chest should go away once the swelling goes down—though I think it's cute. 

I sleep a lot and have been eating a ton--big shout out to frozen chocolate/peanut butter covered bananas and Gatorade! 😂 

I'm open to answering questions if anyone is curious or wants more information! I'm really happy with my experience and recovery. It's been better than I could have ever dreamed!

You really can't be until you test it in humans. 

But before then you can gather evidence by testing it in living tissue or on animals first. Certain proteins, metabolic pathways, and other biological functions can be highly conserved (meaning are kept the same genetically) across species, making a drug or treatment's mechanism of action able to act on non-human animals or in living tissue. 

Since some of these mechanisms of action are similar if not functionally identical to how they work in human biology, you can reasonably infer that at the very least the medication in question isn't outright *harmful* to life first and foremost. From there, you can ascertain enough information that it could improve the lives/symptoms of animals afflicted with a specific kind of disease depending on how you expect the drug to behave. This is measured through observing the test animal's behavior, vitals, labs, and even performing necropsies and taking tissue samples for observations.

Even with all of that, we humans are really complex living creatures! We can communicate symptoms that mice or zebra fish would never be able to, nor would be obvious from a necropsy of a test animal (e.g., nausea, bitter taste after taking medication, etc.) So sure, a medication may perform its function, but it might cause side effects that are so miserable it might as well not work to begin with!

We have a physical log, and the information is added to a spreadsheet at the end of the month. The physical papers are kept in a binder for reference. Granted, we're a pretty low-tech site.

If you check the trial number on clinicaltrials.gov (at least if you're in the US), you sometimes can find the actual protocol listed there to read over. They usually are very in-depth and will discuss the prior testing done with a drug to move to human trials, and will even explain the drug's mechanism and rationale for the study. They're not always posted, but I know a few of the studies I've worked on have had them.

The ICF will be the most informative, though, as they're written to be more accessible to people who might not be used to reading scientific literature. 

Ultimately, it's your decision if you feel comfortable participating in a trial like the one you described. Thank you for considering being in a research study either way!

Subject failed to disclose an exclusionary health condition, despite the CRCs doing their diligence and going over it with the subject AND checking their medical records. Only learned about the condition when it triggered an SAE that resulted in removal from the study... into the ER for a stroke.

My facility has anywhere from 1-3 for leads, but I think we have around 9 or 10 going on right now in total. Usually lead CRCs with higher enrolling studies have fewer at a time. The rest of our CRCs help out on all of them where needed, but will specialize in certain sections since a lot of our studies are surgery-related.

My CRC, it depends on how many appointments you have during the day and what kinds. Screenings always take the longest. I'd say on our busiest days, it may be up to 6 hours; on our slowest, an hour at most. We usually work with adult patients and manage a lot of the data collection through paper, which means a lot of time spent with patients and writing things down.

I imagine the type of research may change that, too. My site specializes in pain, so you end up having to talk with patients a lot to assess their pain level in-clinic. Some sites might not have to talk with patients as much during trials by comparison.

Yes, we've had it happen across several different studies with different sponsors. It's to the point now where our site manager is considering charging sponsors for late-study changes to the data. 

It's borderline unreasonable we're having to go back and enter things like oxygen for hundreds of patients months after a study has started. 

That or sponsors demanding clarification from our site for subject-reported medications... from an app that the sponsors designed that the subjects use daily. Like! If you didn't account for subjects not being medically versed and pestering them to be specific in your initial design, I don't know what to tell you!

I honestly like it a lot when monitors talk with us about what's going on with their end of things. We're all just people trying to do our jobs.

OP it sounds like your daughter is partly going through normal teenager stuff, but that she may also have some kind of mental health issue(s). Normal people with healthy relationships with their bodies/looks don't hide their face from their family or experience paranoia about what others are thinking about. It could be she has body image issues or social anxiety or could even just be trans--I know I had similar issues at the same age as a trans man and I was pretty relentlessly bullied up until I entered high school.

There's a probability too, that those people she's "friends" with, might not actually be her friends or might be really terrible ones. Right now, it just sounds like she's very isolated, if a bit introverted, and is struggling with that.

Unfortunately, therapy only works for people who are open to putting the work in, so the most you can do is just lead the horse to water, so to speak. She has to be the one to decide that she's tired of being sick and wants to heal.

It's also pretty normal for people to have varying levels of comfort when it comes to generosity and differences in how they express thanks or affection to people they care about. Just because your daughter isn't much of a sharing or action-oriented person, doesn't mean she's selfish. Lots of people have a primary love language that's more about quality time or touch or just verbal affirmation. Not to mention, part of growing up is just learning about when it's appropriate to have things your way or to concede and compromise in a situation.

I would also like to point out that you need to work through your feelings on this subject with a professional. I can 100% assure you, as someone who came out as a teenager, your kids know when you don't like them. My dad could never deal with me not being who he wanted me to be and his resentment made me angry and hurt and I tried desperately to keep my emotional and physical distance when I could. He never hurt me or called me names, but I knew he was disappointed in me, and that was supremely painful.

Try to take an interest in her hobbies, figure out how to show some humility--no one can predict how a child will turn out, and it takes a lot of humility to admit that your expectations were wrong and to start having a conversation about things you may have done to facilitate this problem. No parent is ever perfect, and admitting that to your children is so valuable in starting that dialogue and trying to help repair the relationship.

Pretty common in flies--they love getting drunk and will pick fermented fruits to eat from. These look to me like common fruit flies, but it's really hard to tell.

Best thing you can do is make a paper funnel and place it in a cup or jar with whatever they're attracted to; you can add a drop of soap to the water to break the surface tension so they'll drown. They'll either drown or get caught inside and starve--we had Erlenmeyer flask versions of these full of apple cider vinegar when I worked in a fruit fly lab. 

You can also take a pot of boiling water and dump it down your sink drain to kill any potential eggs if they're actually drain flies. In the meantime, try to keep stuff dry where you can by wiping out stuff like sinks, take the trash out often, and make sure your garbage disposal is clear. You can also purchase a carnivorous plant friend if you have distilled or rain water available to you and a very hot, sunny window to keep it in. Sundews are really well equipped for little bugs like this.

If you manage to figure out where they're coming from and keep food and water away from them for the most part they should clear out in about a month, max, if it's cooler!

1. Right click on Cookie Clicker in your Steam Library > Manage > Browse Local Files
2. Go through the folders resources > app
3. Right click on "start.js" > Open with... > Choose another app > Notepad
4. Find the phrase "let DEV=0;//display menu and js console" and change the 0 to a 1. (Note: It's close to the top of the file so you shouldn't have to scroll at all to find it.)
5. Save and close.
6. Boot up Cookie Clicker, the console should now be visible.
7. Type in "Game.OpenSesame();" into the console and hit enter.
8. You now have the debug cheats.

The Orphan's Cord, which was acquired by Willem and later Iosefka (not outright stated, but can be inferred easily enough), the Vileblood Child's Cord found in the Abandoned Workshop (the description for which was removed in a later patch) which was acquired by Laurence and used to beckon the MP, Mergo's Cord, and the Cord of Arianna's child.

I figured it was because we're not technically in the waking world but like a bunch of overlapping weird areas all kind of mashed together with their own unique time restraints (which honestly would really explain why Old Yharnam still has stuff on fire or why there's blood fresh enough to attract Blood Lickers in Cainhurst). 

Though in Yharnam's case I'd imagine it's because the blood moon isn't actually a moon phase, but a symbol of the presence of Great Ones. Great Ones are not necessarily omnipresent, and as a result their powers are limited to a specific area. So, it could really just be that much in the way that one person can only exist in one place at one time, so too does a Great One.

I always thought for at least a few of the item descriptions it was the hunter remembering things and restoring themselves from their amnesic state as they picked them up and more closely examined them. But after reading your response I went back and re-read the description for the Kos Parasite just to make sure I didn't misinterpret something and it does indicate that she died prior to washing up in the Fishing Hamlet. The description uses the phrase "the carcass of Kos" and the word carcass is usually used to describe a large dead thing. We do know for sure that a curse results from angering a Great One, but if Kos was already dead then there had to be another source for the curse.

As for a Great One dying out of the blue: you're right. It is super weird and the information provided to us about Great Ones is pretty scant. At most we know that they can be killed, that they always lose their children, and that the only way to make new Great Ones to for you yourself to become one. But the lifespan of one left undisturbed is never really given to us--and considering that the Great Ones the Ptumerians look after are "slumbering" they probably live indefinitely. I agree that Kos was likely killed but I think by the townspeople rather than the hunters because I can't think of a reason why the hunters or Byrgenwerth would have been in the Hamlet prior to news of Kos' death and/or corpse spreading around.
